title: What capability and training evidence does the Financial Accountability Regime expect of accountable persons?
description: How the Financial Accountability Regime Act 2023 applies to banks, insurers and super trustees, and what capability evidence supports reasonable steps.
shortAnswer: The Financial Accountability Regime Act 2023 (FAR) requires Australian banks, insurers and superannuation trustees, and their accountable persons, to act with honesty, integrity, due skill, care and diligence and to take reasonable steps to prevent prudential harm and material contraventions. FAR sets no training hours, but section 22 defines reasonable steps as appropriate governance, controls and remediation, so documented onboarding, capability assessment and briefing records are central evidence.
keyTakeaways: FAR is jointly administered by the Australian Prudential Regulation Authority (APRA) and the Australian Securities and Investments Commission (ASIC), and replaced the Banking Executive Accountability Regime (BEAR).
It applied to authorized deposit-taking institutions (ADIs) from March 15, 2024, and to general insurers, life companies, private health insurers and RSE licensees from March 15, 2025.

Section 21 sets four accountability obligations for accountable persons, and section 22 says reasonable steps include appropriate governance, control and risk management, safeguards against inappropriate delegation, and procedures to identify and remediate problems.

The Minister rules make senior executive responsibility for the human resource, compliance, breach reporting and anti-money laundering functions prescribed responsibilities, so capability programs have a named accountable owner.
Since October 16, 2026, ASIC asks AFS licensees for less evidence of competence when a responsible manager is also a FAR accountable person.
regulator: Australian Prudential Regulation Authority (APRA) and Australian Securities and Investments Commission (ASIC), jointly
appliesTo: ADIs and authorized non-operating holding companies (NOHCs) of ADIs
General insurers, life companies, private health insurers and their relevant NOHCs
Directors and senior executives who are accountable persons, and significant related entities of accountable entities

sections.heading: Who does FAR apply to, and from when?

blocks.text: FAR applies to accountable entities in banking, insurance and superannuation and to the individuals who hold senior executive accountability within them. APRA's [FAR overview](https://www.apra.gov.au/cross-industry/financial-accountability-regime-far) says the regime commenced for ADIs and their authorized NOHCs from March 15, 2024, and for insurance entities, their licensed NOHCs and superannuation trustees from March 15, 2025. Section 9 of the [Financial Accountability Regime Act 2023](https://www.legislation.gov.au/C2023A00067/latest/text) sets these as 6 and 18 months after the Act commenced.

An accountable person is someone who, because of their position, has actual or effective senior executive responsibility for management or control of the entity or of a significant or substantial part of its operations (section 10(1)), or who holds a responsibility or position prescribed by the Minister rules. Under section 5 of the [Financial Accountability Regime (Minister) Rules 2024](https://www.legislation.gov.au/F2024L00283/latest/text), board members are prescribed positions, and prescribed responsibilities include senior executive responsibility for financial resources or operations, risk management, information management, internal audit, compliance, the human resource function, dispute resolution, remediation programs, breach reporting and, for AML/CTF reporting entities, the anti-money laundering function.

Sector specific responsibilities are added on top. For insurers, the actuarial and claims handling functions are prescribed. For RSE licensees, member administration, the investment function, the financial advice service and insurance offerings are prescribed. Trustee governance and fit and proper requirements that sit alongside FAR are covered on the [APRA superannuation governance and fit and proper](/regulations/apra-superannuation-sps-510-fit-and-proper-training) page.

blocks.title: Currency
blocks.text: This page reflects the FAR Act (compilation of February 21, 2025), the Minister rules as made in 2024, the joint regulators' information paper updated on July 11, 2024, and ASIC guidance as at November 2026. Check the Federal Register of Legislation for later amendments before relying on a section number.

sections.heading: What are the accountability obligations under section 21?

blocks.text: Section 21(1) requires an accountable person to conduct the responsibilities of their position in four ways, and each one implies a capability an entity should be able to show it has built and tested.

items: Acting "with honesty and integrity, and with due skill, care and diligence".
Dealing with the Regulator in an open, constructive and cooperative way.
Taking reasonable steps to prevent matters from arising that would, or would be likely to, adversely affect the entity's prudential standing or prudential reputation.

Taking reasonable steps to prevent matters that would, or would be likely to, result in a material contravention by the entity of listed laws, including the FAR Act, the Banking Act 1959, the credit legislation, the financial services law, the Insurance Act 1973, the Life Insurance Act 1995 and the Superannuation Industry (Supervision) Act 1993.

blocks.text: Section 21(2) adds that where two or more accountable persons share a responsibility, each carries the full obligation as if it were theirs alone. Entities have parallel obligations: the joint [information paper for accountable entities](https://www.apra.gov.au/news-and-publications/financial-accountability-regime-information-accountable-entities) says an accountable entity must take reasonable steps to conduct its business with honesty, integrity, due skill, care and diligence, deal openly with the Regulators, prevent matters adversely affecting its prudential standing, and ensure each accountable person meets their obligations.

sections.heading: What counts as reasonable steps, and where does training fit?

blocks.text: FAR does not mention training, but its statutory description of reasonable steps is where capability evidence matters most. Section 22 says, without limiting the concept, that taking reasonable steps includes:

items: having appropriate governance, control and risk management in relation to the matter;
having safeguards against inappropriate delegations of responsibility;
having appropriate procedures for identifying and remediating problems that arise or may arise; and
taking appropriate action in response to non-compliance or suspected non-compliance.

blocks.text: Each limb has a capability dimension. An accountable person who delegates a function needs evidence that the delegate was competent for it, which is the "safeguards against inappropriate delegations" limb. A problem identification procedure only works if the staff running it can recognize a problem, and an executive responsible for breach reporting needs staff who can spot a reportable breach. Training records alone do not prove any of this, which is why assessment results and observed performance carry more weight than completions, as explained in [completion tracking vs competency verification](/compare/completion-tracking-vs-competency-verification).

The prescribed human resource function responsibility also means that one accountable person owns the entity's people capability arrangements, including mandatory training. That person needs management information showing coverage, overdue training and assessment outcomes by role, in the form described in [how to report training compliance to the board](/guides/how-to-report-training-compliance-to-the-board).

sections.heading: What must happen before someone becomes an accountable person?

blocks.text: The entity must register the person with the Regulators, declare that it is satisfied the person is suitable, and for larger entities lodge an accountability statement, all before the person takes up the role unless a grace period applies. The information paper says registration is made through APRA Connect, that the Regulators expect the suitability declaration to be made by the chair of the relevant board committee or a delegate, and that an application meeting all requirements is deemed registered 21 days after it is lodged.

Grace periods are 90 days for a temporary or unforeseen vacancy and 30 days for a director appointed at a general meeting or an accountable person of a newly licensed entity. The Regulators expect applications at least 21 days before the person starts or the grace period ends, and say incorrect or missing information can put the entity in breach of its key personnel obligations under section 23. That timetable is the natural window for structured onboarding, set out in [how to structure onboarding for regulated roles](/guides/how-to-structure-onboarding-for-regulated-roles): the suitability declaration is stronger when it rests on a documented capability assessment against the specific responsibilities in the draft accountability statement.

Accountability statements and an accountability map are required only for enhanced entities. The information paper sets the enhanced notification thresholds at total assets of $20 billion for ADIs, $10 billion for general insurers and life companies, $3 billion for private health insurers and $30 billion for RSE licensees, and if one entity in a group is enhanced, all accountable entities in the group are. The initial map is due within 30 days of becoming an accountable entity, and material changes to statements or the map must be lodged within 30 days.

sections.heading: How do FAR obligations map to capability evidence?

blocks.text: The table below is an original, illustrative mapping of FAR obligations to the role that carries them, a sensible frequency and the evidence a regulator reviewing reasonable steps would expect to see. FAR prescribes none of these frequencies; they are policy choices an entity should document and justify.

blocks.text: For each record, keep the version of the accountability statement the person was assessed against. When a statement changes materially, the gap between old and new responsibilities defines the retraining required, and an [audit trail](/glossary/audit-trail) linking the two is the evidence that the entity responded.

sections.heading: What are the consequences of falling short?

blocks.text: Entities face civil penalties, and accountable persons face disqualification and loss of deferred variable remuneration. Under section 83, the maximum penalty for a body corporate is the greatest of 50,000 penalty units, three times the benefit derived or detriment avoided, or 10% of annual turnover capped at 2.5 million penalty units. A note to section 83 says section 81, on ancillary contraventions, is the only civil penalty provision that can be contravened by a person other than a body corporate.

The information paper says the Regulators may disqualify an individual who has breached their accountability obligations (section 42), issue directions to an entity, and accept court enforceable undertakings. Entities must defer at least 40% of an accountable person's variable remuneration for at least four years and have a remuneration policy that reduces it for a failure to meet accountability obligations. They must also notify the Regulators when an accountable person is dismissed, suspended or has variable remuneration reduced for such a failure.

sections.heading: How does FAR interact with ASIC responsible manager requirements?

blocks.text: Where a FAR accountable person is also a responsible manager on an Australian financial services license, ASIC now asks for less evidence of competence in licensing applications. ASIC's [RG 105 page](https://asic.gov.au/regulatory-resources/find-a-document/regulatory-guides/rg-105-licensing-organisational-competence/) says the changes took effect on the ASIC Regulatory Portal on October 16, 2026, streamline responsible manager requirements for entities subject to the FAR Act, and that an updated guide is expected in Quarter 1 of 2027.

The practical effect is that the entity's own FAR suitability process carries more of the competence burden. The organizational competence obligation itself is unchanged, as explained on the [ASIC RG 105 organizational competence](/regulations/asic-rg-105-organisational-competence) page, so the capability assessment behind the FAR declaration should be detailed enough to stand in for evidence ASIC no longer collects. For the operational risk side of the same executives' roles, see [APRA CPS 230 and staff capability](/regulations/apra-cps-230-operational-risk-training).

sections.heading: How does Knowledge Foundry approach this?

blocks.text: Knowledge Foundry treats each accountability statement as a structured set of responsibilities, links each one to the knowledge and judgment it requires, and records which version a person was assessed against. When responsibilities are reallocated, the framework shows which capability evidence no longer matches and which assessments need to be repeated.

faqs.q: Does FAR require accountable persons to complete a set number of training hours?
faqs.a: No. The FAR Act and Minister rules set no training hours or course content. The obligations are framed as honesty, integrity, due skill, care and diligence, and reasonable steps, and section 22 describes reasonable steps in terms of governance, controls, delegation safeguards and remediation. Training and assessment records are one way to evidence those, not a stand alone requirement.

faqs.q: Do the Regulators approve accountable persons?
faqs.a: No. The joint information paper says the Regulators do not approve registration applications, although they may ask for more information. The entity is responsible for assessing suitability and declaring it, and a complete application is deemed registered 21 days after lodgement.

faqs.q: Are core entities exempt from accountability statements?
faqs.a: Core entities do not have to submit accountability statements or maps; only entities above the enhanced notification thresholds do. The information paper still encourages all accountable entities to document their accountability arrangements, including how they comply with their key personnel obligations, which is where capability evidence usually sits.

faqs.q: Who owns mandatory training under FAR?
faqs.a: The Minister rules prescribe senior executive responsibility for an entity's human resource function and its compliance function as responsibilities that make the holder an accountable person. Mandatory training usually falls under one or both, so a named accountable person should own its coverage and effectiveness.

FAR Act s9: ADIs are accountable entities from 6 months after commencement; general insurers, life companies, private health insurers and RSE licensees from 18 months; s10(1) defines accountable person by actual or effective senior executive responsibility

FAR Act s21(1)(a) to (d) accountability obligations, including the list of laws in s21(1)(d); s21(2) shared responsibilities; s22 reasonable steps includes governance, control and risk management, safeguards against inappropriate delegations, procedures for identifying and remediating problems, and action on non-compliance

FAR Act s83: body corporate maximum is greatest of 50,000 penalty units, 3 times benefit, or 10% of annual turnover capped at 2.5 million penalty units; note says s81 is the only civil penalty provision a person other than a body corporate can contravene

Minister Rules s5 prescribed responsibilities include financial resources or operations, risk, information management, internal audit, compliance, human resource function, dispute resolution, remediation, breach reporting and AML function; s6 board members prescribed; s7 actuarial and claims handling for insurers; s8 member administration, investment, financial advice and insurance offerings for RSE licensees

Registration via APRA Connect with suitability declaration expected from board committee chair; deemed registered 21 days after application; grace periods 90 days (temporary or unforeseen vacancy) and 30 days (director appointed at general meeting, newly licensed entity); Regulators do not approve applications

Enhanced notification thresholds: ADIs $20 billion, general insurers and life companies $10 billion, private health insurers $3 billion, RSE licensees $30 billion; group rule; initial accountability map within 30 days; material changes within 30 days

Deferral of at least 40% of variable remuneration for minimum four years; remuneration policy requiring reduction; notification of dismissal, suspension or remuneration reduction; disqualification under s42
